data.title: The magnate's burial mound Holásky 2 – a Hallstatt warrior's grave
data.excerpt: Holásky near Brno became famous for the discovery of large magnates' burial mounds of the Horákov culture of the Hallstatt period. Our 3D reconstruction brings to life the oak burial chamber of mound number 2, measuring 5 × 5 m, in which a warrior lay with two iron spears, embossed bronze bowls and three unique iron spits.
data.metaTitle: Holásky 2 – a Hallstatt magnate's burial mound

children.text: Holásky is a former village, today a city district of Brno – Tuřany, which became famous for the discovery of large magnates' burial mounds of the so-called Horákov culture of the Hallstatt period. This culture represents a continuous development from the end of the Bronze Age, through the Hallstatt period, down to the beginning of the La Tène period (in terms of time this covers the end of the 8th to the beginning of the 4th century BC). We recognise the culture in the territory of southern Moravia, where it is regarded as the direct successor of the Podolí culture (the Final Bronze Age, part of the Middle Danube urnfield group of cultures). The grave assemblages from Brno-Holásky are unique and, by their richness, rank among the burial assemblages of the highest social stratum of the said Horákov culture.

The site itself lies on former fields in the so-called “Krumlové čtvrti” (the Krumlov quarter). The magnates' burial mounds of the Hallstatt period were discovered here in the 1920s. The first mound appeared in the field as a large hill made of black earth, which the inhabitants of the village mistakenly believed to date from the period of the Napoleonic wars. The archaeologist Ladislav Červinka was alerted to the spot in 1925. After inspecting the feature he recognised in it a prehistoric burial mound, which, as he subsequently established, was not standing alone. In its vicinity he discovered two more. Despite the fact that the mounds had been damaged by ploughing, the mound of the first of them reached a width of as much as 70 metres in the 1920s. Originally the mounds were probably higher and less spread out in width. After these initial observations, excavation began, and during it 2 grave chambers of oak wood were discovered in 2 of the mounds, measuring 5.25 × 5.30 m and 5 × 5 m. The third mound was not investigated until several years later. 
 
 Together with Dwarf Digital Archeology and with the generous help of the archaeologist Martin Golec and the archaeology student Zuzana Mírová, we have attempted to reconstruct the possible appearance of burial mound number 2. The chamber of this mound was oriented on a north–south axis and had dimensions similar to those of the first mound. It lay about 25 metres away from it. At the time of the excavation the mound was about 1 metre high and the burial chamber was sunk 1 metre below the ground surface. Beside the western wall of the chamber lay the skeleton of a man. Judging by the grave goods, he was a warrior. His head was placed to the north; the skull survived, and above it 4 bronze rings had been set out. On his right side lay 2 iron spears, on his left side two embossed bronze bowls with a rim worked in a beaded pattern. Behind them were three unique iron spits, which evidently point to Etruscan influences in the Horákov culture. In the south-eastern corner there were pottery vessels and a bronze ladle. 
 
 On the basis of analogies from other magnates' graves of the Hallstatt period, we assume that the dead man probably lay on a wooden bier and also had a larger quantity of supplies and food in the burial chamber, which was evidently connected with ideas about a funeral feast of the deceased in the afterlife, and this in turn was connected with a firm belief in life after death.
